root.note: Wiktionary glosses tomatl as tomatillo; the red tomato was xītomatl. What the parts of the Nahuatl word meant is less clear: one source suggests ‘fat water’.

history: Spain's gazpacho and pan con tomate rest on a Mexican word. Spaniards brought the fruit to Europe after the conquest, and with it Nahuatl tomatl, whose ending became -ate as in many Mexican words. In Nahuatl tomatl meant the green fruit we call a tomatillo; the red one was xītomatl. That difference lives on in Mexico, where jitomate is usually the red tomato and tomate may be green, so check before you order there. In Spain tomate is simply tomato. Spanish then spread the word through Europe. Italy preferred pomodoro, ‘golden apple’, and Russian took pomidor from that.
historyEinfach: Tomate is a word from Mexico. The Aztecs spoke Nahuatl, and their word was tomatl. Spaniards brought the fruit and the word to Europe. Then many languages took the word from Spanish. In Mexico, a red tomato is often called jitomate. In Spain, it is always tomate. In Italy, it is pomodoro, ‘golden apple’.

elsewhere.text: English tomato and potato sound alike, and both came through Spanish from America, but they have different origins.
Italian made a new name for the fruit instead of borrowing one, and Russian took it from Italian.
